newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - IBM reports solid second quarter results.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - IBM reports solid second quarter results.

text.p: International Business Machines Corp. on Monday reported slightly higher earnings for the second quarter as strong demand for services, semiconductors and disk drives offset declining sales in some hardware lines.
The world's largest computer maker said it earned $1.4 billion, or $1.46 a share, in the quarter, up from $1.3 billion, or $1.26 a share a year earlier, adjusted for a two-for-one stock split.
The results came slightly above Wall Street's expectations, but not enough to spark a rally in IBM shares, which often have a big influence on the broader stock market.

"After the runup (in the stock in recent days), it will probably go down," said Bill Milton, a Brown Brothers Harriman analyst. "There was nothing wrong with the numbers. But looking ahead, the operating environment is getting tougher."

IBM stock fell 75 cents to $103.75 on the New York Stock Exchange. It reported results after the close of trading. Analysts had forecast earnings of $1.42 a share on average, according to First Call, which tracks earnings estimates.
"It was a relatively dull quarter compared to some previous quarters," said Steve Milunovich, a Morgan Stanley analyst. "I don't think it was a very surprising quarter.

Milunovich said he will "tweak" his earnings estimates on IBM, but not make any dramatic changes based on this quarter or from the comments by the interim chief financial officer in his first conference call with analysts.

Sales rose 4 percent to $18.9 billion from $18.2 billion, but when reported in constant currencies, IBM said its revenues were up 8 percent. IBM said that currency fluctuations hurt earnings by about 10 cents a share, as the dollar strengthened against some currencies.

"These results show the ongoing strength of our broad business portfolio," IBM Chairman Louis Gerstner said. "We saw very good customer response to our new System/390 servers and continuing strength in services and hard disk drives."

IBM said strong results in some businesses -- services, semiconductors, and hard disk drives -- as well as improved results in mainframes, offset lower revenue in other segments, such as AS/400 minicomputers, RS/6000 workstations and the Aptiva line of personal computers aimed at consumers.

Analysts said they were surprised by mainframe revenues, which were flat as opposed to down. IBM attributed some of the growth in mainframes to its lower prices and customer acceptance of its new G4 systems based on lower-cost microprocessor technology. IBM has completely phased out all manufacturing of its older, more costly, bipolar mainframe.

"The System/390 business improved dramatically," said IBM's interim chief financial officer, Lawrence Ricciardi, in a brief telephone interview. Ricciardi is IBM's interim CFO since G. Richard Thoman, IBM's previous CFO, left last month to become the No. 2 executive at Xerox Corp.

In the first quarter, IBM said that in terms of the amount of mainframe processing power shipped, the number of MIPS (millions of instructions per second) shipped were down 6 percent. This quarter, they were up 60 percent.
IBM does not provide further details on its mainframe business, which is increasingly a smaller part of its overall revenue picture but still a big contributor to profits.

"We didn't expect mainframes to be flat," said John Jones, a Salomon Brothers analyst. "I think what happened is they made some very attractive deals selling the older (G3) models in April and May. ... It was a good quarter, it was solid."

IBM also said results from its commercial PCs and PC servers were "good." Servers link computers, store software and manage data on a network. But its consumer PCs were a major disappointment and helped drag down overall PC sales.
At the IBM PC Co., Ricciardi said IBM's quarterly growth rate fell behind rival Compaq Computer Corp.

"As opposed to last quarter, Compaq grew faster than we did in both in units and revenue," he said. "In gross profit margin, they maintained their lead; in expense-to-revenue, we maintained our lead; and inventory turnover was a toss-up."

Ricciardi said PCs performed well in North America and the Asia-Pacific region but were weak in Europe. He also said the more costly versions of the consumer line were not growing as fast as the lower-cost models.

Also disappointing was the RS/6000 workstation models running the Unix operating system, which are seeing more competition from Windows NT-based PCs that are increasingly infringing on the workstation turf.

New products in the RS/6000 family and in the AS/400 minicomputer line should help the second half of the year, analysts said. Ricciardi said that he is more upbeat about the coming product transition in the AS/400 line, which will introduce new products later this quarter.
Ricciardi said he was pleased with the results and "comfortable" with the outlook for the rest of the year.
"We are performing in line with our long-term objectives," Ricciardi told Wall Street analysts in a conference call.

On an as-reported basis, revenue in North America grew 10 percent to $8.6 billion, Asia-Pacific revenue rose 4 percent to $3.8 billion and Latin America grew 8 percent to $847 million. Revenues from Europe, the Middle East and Africa fell 5 percent to $5.7 billion.

As expected, revenues at the fast-growing services business jumped 24 percent to $4.6 billion. About $3.3 billion in new services contracts were signed in the quarter as the business continued to show strong growth. Software revenues fell 3 percent to $3.1 billion, due to a decline in mainframe software. Revenues in distributed software, such as Lotus Notes and Tivoli systems management software, were strong.

Ricciardi, who is also still juggling his position as IBM's chief counsel, declined to comment on whether he will become the permanent chief financial officer, as some on Wall Street are predicting. He said IBM continues to look both inside and outside the company for suitable candidates.

"I am not taking myself out, nor am I putting myself in (the running)," Ricciardi said. "I will do it as long as it makes sense to do it," he told analysts, joking that he could be Wall Street's greatest nightmare, a lawyer delivering financial news.
